Lab Assignment 10 — Semantic IR Using LSA and Word2Vec¶

IT550: Information Retrieval · Instructor: Prof. Sandip Modha Student ID: 202303022

This notebook builds and evaluates

  1. a TF-IDF vector-space baseline on the Cranfield collection (Part 1),
  2. a Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) retrieval system using truncated SVD (Part 2),
  3. an evaluation and dimensionality analysis of LSA against the baseline with P@5, MAP and nDCG@10 (Part 3),
  4. Word2Vec embeddings (CBOW and Skip-gram), compared with count-based (TF-IDF and PPMI co-occurrence) word similarity (Part 4).

All results below were produced by running the notebook top to bottom. Rankings, tables, figures and a machine-readable results.json are written to outputs/.

Dataset: Cranfield collection¶

  • cran.all.1400 — 1,400 aerodynamics abstracts with fields .I (id), .T (title), .A (author), .B (bibliography), .W (abstract).
  • cran.qry — 225 queries. The .I numbers in this file are not consecutive (001, 002, 004, …); cranqrel numbers the queries 1–225 in file order, so query i in cranqrel is the i-th query of cran.qry.
  • cranqrel — lines query doc grade. Grades: 1 = most relevant … 4 = minimal interest, and −1 (one per query).

As required by the lab:

  • a document is relevant for P@5 and MAP if its grade is 1, 2 or 3;
  • the nDCG gain is 4 − grade (grade 1 → 3, grade 2 → 2, grade 3 → 1, grade 4 → 0); grade −1 is not relevant and gets no gain;
  • only queries with at least one relevant document are evaluated.
In [2]:
def parse_cran_docs(path):
    docs, cur, field = [], None, None
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
        tag = line.strip()
        if line.startswith(".I"):
            if cur is not None:
                docs.append(cur)
            cur = {"doc_id": int(line.split()[1]), "T": [], "A": [], "B": [], "W": []}
            field = None
        elif tag in (".T", ".A", ".B", ".W"):
            field = tag[1]
        elif field is not None:
            cur[field].append(tag)
    docs.append(cur)
    return pd.DataFrame([{"doc_id": d["doc_id"],
                          "title": " ".join(d["T"]).strip(),
                          "abstract": " ".join(d["W"]).strip()} for d in docs])


def parse_cran_queries(path):
    queries, cur, field = [], None, None
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
        tag = line.strip()
        if line.startswith(".I"):
            if cur is not None:
                queries.append(cur)
            cur = {"orig_id": int(line.split()[1]), "W": []}
            field = None
        elif tag == ".W":
            field = "W"
        elif field is not None:
            cur["W"].append(tag)
    queries.append(cur)
    # cranqrel numbers the queries 1..225 in file order
    return pd.DataFrame([{"qid": i + 1, "orig_id": q["orig_id"], "text": " ".join(q["W"]).strip()}
                         for i, q in enumerate(queries)])

qrels_df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "cranqrel", sep=r"\s+", header=None, names=["qid", "doc_id", "grade"])

Part 1 — Corpus preparation and TF-IDF baseline¶

Preprocessing pipeline (identical for documents and queries):

  1. lower-casing;
  2. tokenisation with the regular expression [a-z]+ (splits on punctuation, hyphens and digits);
  3. stop-word removal with scikit-learn's English stop-word list (318 words) and removal of 1-character tokens;
  4. Porter stemming (NLTK).
In [4]:
STOP = frozenset(ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS)
TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[a-z]+")
stemmer = PorterStemmer()
_stem_cache = {}

def tokenize(text):
    # steps 1-3: lowercase, tokenise, drop stop words and 1-character tokens
    return [t for t in TOKEN_RE.findall(text.lower()) if t not in STOP and len(t) > 1]

def stem(token):
    if token not in _stem_cache:
        _stem_cache[token] = stemmer.stem(token)
    return _stem_cache[token]

def preprocess(text):
    # full pipeline used as the TfidfVectorizer analyzer
    return [stem(t) for t in tokenize(text)]

example = queries_df.loc[0, "text"]
print("raw      :", example)
print("tokens   :", tokenize(example))
print("stemmed  :", preprocess(example))

doc_tokens = [preprocess(t) for t in docs_df["text"]]
doc_lens = np.array([len(t) for t in doc_tokens])
print(f"\ntokens per document after preprocessing: mean {doc_lens.mean():.1f}, median {np.median(doc_lens):.0f}, "
      f"total {doc_lens.sum():,}")

TF-IDF document–term matrix. TfidfVectorizer with the analyzer above, raw term frequency, smoothed IDF idf(t) = ln((1+N)/(1+df(t))) + 1 and L2-normalised rows. The vectorizer is fitted on the documents only; queries are transformed with the same vocabulary and IDF weights (transform), so out-of-vocabulary query terms are ignored.

def rank_all(sim):
    # sim: queries x docs. Returns doc ids ranked by descending score (ties broken by doc id).
    order = np.argsort(-sim, axis=1, kind="stable")
    return order + 1, np.take_along_axis(sim, order, axis=1)

def save_top10(ranked, scores, run_name):
    rows = []
    for i, qid in enumerate(queries_df["qid"]):
        for r in range(10):
            rows.append((qid, queries_df.loc[i, "orig_id"], r + 1, int(ranked[i, r]), float(scores[i, r])))
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["qid", "orig_query_id", "rank", "doc_id", "score"])
    df.to_csv(OUT / "rankings" / f"{run_name}_top10.csv", index=False)
    # the same ranking in TREC run format: qid Q0 docid rank score tag
    with open(OUT / "rankings" / f"{run_name}_top10.trec", "w") as f:
        for r in df.itertuples(index=False):
            f.write(f"{r.qid} Q0 {r.doc_id} {r.rank} {r.score:.6f} {run_name}\n")
    return df

query_times = []
for _ in range(3):                                  # median of 3 runs
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    sim_tfidf = cosine_similarity(Q, X)             # 225 x 1400

Part 2 — Truncated SVD and the LSA representation¶

The TF-IDF matrix is factorised as $X \approx U_k \Sigma_k V_k^\top$ (documents × terms). Documents are represented in the $k$-dimensional latent space by $X V_k = U_k\Sigma_k$ and a query vector $q$ is folded into the same space by $q V_k$ (this is exactly TruncatedSVD.fit_transform / transform). Documents are then ranked by cosine similarity in that space.

$k = 50$ is valid here: it is far below $\min(1400, |V|) - 1$.

In [7]:
def run_lsa(k, seed=SEED, repeats=3):
    # runtimes are the median over `repeats` identical runs
    assert 0 < k < min(X.shape), f"k={k} is not valid for a {X.shape} matrix"
    fit_times, query_times = [], []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=k, algorithm="randomized", n_iter=10, random_state=seed)
        D_k = svd.fit_transform(X)                # documents in latent space (= U_k Sigma_k)
        fit_times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        Q_k = svd.transform(Q)                    # queries folded in (= q V_k)
        sim = cosine_similarity(Q_k, D_k)
        ranked, scores = rank_all(sim)
        query_times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    fit_time, query_time = float(np.median(fit_times)), float(np.median(query_times))
    energy = float((svd.singular_values_ ** 2).sum() / X.multiply(X).sum())
    return dict(k=k, svd=svd, D=D_k, Q=Q_k, sim=sim, ranked=ranked, scores=scores, fit_time=fit_time,
                query_time=query_time, explained_variance=float(svd.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()),
                energy=energy)

K_MAIN = 50
lsa50 = run_lsa(K_MAIN)
top10_lsa50 = save_top10(lsa50["ranked"], lsa50["scores"], f"lsa_k{K_MAIN}")

Part 3 — Evaluation and dimensionality analysis¶

Metrics (averaged over the evaluated queries):

  • P@5 — fraction of the top 5 documents that are relevant (grade 1–3).
  • MAP — mean of average precision computed over the full ranking of all 1,400 documents (standard, uncut AP). Because only top-10 lists are saved, MAP@10 (AP over the top 10, divided by min(|R|, 10)) is reported too.
  • nDCG@10 — $\mathrm{DCG@10} = \sum_{i=1}^{10} \frac{gain_i}{\log_2(i+1)}$ with $gain = 4 - grade$, normalised by the DCG of the ideal ordering of all judged relevant documents.
In [10]:
def precision_at(ranked, rel, k=5):
    return len(set(ranked[:k]) & rel) / k

def average_precision(ranked, rel, cutoff=None):
    hits, s = 0, 0.0
    for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:cutoff] if cutoff else ranked, start=1):
        if d in rel:
            hits += 1
            s += hits / i
    denom = min(len(rel), cutoff) if cutoff else len(rel)
    return s / denom

def ndcg_at(ranked, g, k=10):
    dcg = sum(g.get(d, 0) / np.log2(i + 2) for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:k]))
    ideal = sorted(g.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(v / np.log2(i + 2) for i, v in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg

def evaluate(ranked):
    # ranked: (225, n_docs) array of doc ids. Returns per-query metrics for evaluated queries.
    rows = []
    for qid in eval_qids:
        r = ranked[qid - 1].tolist()
        rows.append({"qid": qid, "P@5": precision_at(r, relevant[qid], 5),
                     "MAP": average_precision(r, relevant[qid]),
                     "MAP@10": average_precision(r, relevant[qid], cutoff=10),
                     "nDCG@10": ndcg_at(r, gains[qid], 10)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("qid")

# sanity checks of the metric code on a toy ranking
assert precision_at([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {1, 3}) == 0.4
assert abs(average_precision([1, 9, 3], {1, 3}) - (1 + 2/3) / 2) < 1e-12
assert abs(ndcg_at([5, 6], {5: 3, 6: 2}) - 1.0) < 1e-12

def side_by_side(qid):
    rows = []
    for r in range(10):
        dt, dl = int(ranked_tfidf[qid - 1, r]), int(lsa50["ranked"][qid - 1, r])
        mark = lambda d: f"{d}{' *R' + str(4 - gains[qid][d]) if d in relevant[qid] else ''}"
        rows.append({"rank": r + 1, "TF-IDF": mark(dt), "LSA k=50": mark(dl)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("rank")

Observations (top-10 comparison). The two systems agree on only about half of each top-10 list (5.2 documents on average, Jaccard 0.38), so LSA is not just re-ordering the TF-IDF ranking. For query 1 both systems put doc 51 first. LSA adds the relevant docs 102 and 876, which TF-IDF misses, and drops 879.

def query_term_overlap(qid, doc_id):
    # query stems that literally occur in the document
    q = set(preprocess(queries_df.loc[qid - 1, "text"]))
    return sorted(q & set(doc_tokens[doc_id - 1]))

def explain(qid):
    qtext = queries_df.loc[qid - 1, "text"]
    print(f"qid {qid} (cran.qry .I {queries_df.loc[qid-1,'orig_id']}): {qtext}")
    print("query stems:", preprocess(qtext))
    t10, l10 = set(ranked_tfidf[qid - 1, :10]), set(lsa50["ranked"][qid - 1, :10])
    rows = []
    for d in sorted(relevant[qid], key=lambda d: -gains[qid][d]):
        rt_ = int(np.where(ranked_tfidf[qid - 1] == d)[0][0]) + 1
        rl_ = int(np.where(lsa50["ranked"][qid - 1] == d)[0][0]) + 1
        rows.append({"doc": d, "grade": 4 - gains[qid][d], "rank TF-IDF": rt_, "rank LSA": rl_,
                     "cos TF-IDF": round(float(sim_tfidf[qid - 1, d - 1]), 3),
                     "shared query stems": " ".join(query_term_overlap(qid, d)),
                     "title": docs_df.loc[d - 1, "title"][:70]})
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("doc"))
    return t10, l10

# Does LSA help most when the relevant documents share few words with the query?
# For every (query, relevant doc) pair, compare the rank given by each system, bucketed by literal overlap.
rows = []

    qs = set(preprocess(queries_df.loc[q - 1, "text"]))
    pos_t = np.empty(n_docs, int); pos_t[ranked_tfidf[q - 1] - 1] = np.arange(1, n_docs + 1)
    pos_l = np.empty(n_docs, int); pos_l[lsa50["ranked"][q - 1] - 1] = np.arange(1, n_docs + 1)
    for d in relevant[q]:

Discussion — where LSA helps and where it hurts (k = 50).

Improvement — qid 184, "work on small-oscillation re-entry motions" (nDCG@10 0.00 → 0.70, AP 0.10 → 0.60). The relevant documents describe the same physics with different words: "dynamic stability of vehicles traversing ascending or descending paths" (doc 67), "oscillatory motion of manned vehicles entering the earth's atmosphere" (doc 716), "oscillations of a vehicle entering a planetary atmosphere" (doc 499). The query stem entri (from re-entry) never matches enter, and generic words such as work and small add noise, so TF-IDF ranks these documents 13th–94th. In the latent space, missile, vehicle, descending, atmosphere, oscillation, motion load on the same dimensions, so LSA moves doc 67 from rank 57 to 1 and doc 716 from 20 to 2. This is the synonymy problem that LSA is designed to solve.

Degradation — qid 136, "creep buckling of round tubes under external pressure" (AP 1.00 → 0.13). There is a single relevant document (1021), and TF-IDF ranks it first because it shares five stems with the query. The collection holds a dense cluster of creep buckling papers (950, 951, 1013, 1017, 1031, …). With only 50 dimensions they collapse onto almost the same latent vector, and the specific words that single out the relevant paper (tubes, round, external pressure) are averaged away. Doc 1021 drops to rank 8. The other large losses follow the same pattern: qid 148 (sandwich cylinders), qid 5 (chemical kinetic systems) and qid 9 (slip flow heat transfer) are all precise queries whose key term is rare and discriminative. Truncating the SVD discards that fine-grained information. This is the precision cost of LSA: it merges related topics.

Quantitative evidence. The table above groups every (query, relevant document) pair by how many of the query's stems literally occur in the document. When a relevant document shares at most 20 % of the query stems, LSA ranks it higher than TF-IDF in 72.6 % of the cases (median rank 397 → 188). When it shares more than 60 %, TF-IDF wins and LSA ranks it higher only 28.8 % of the time (median rank 4 vs 6.5). LSA helps on vocabulary mismatch and hurts on queries that exact matching already answers well.

3.3 Repeating LSA with different numbers of dimensions¶

The lab asks for two or three values such as 20, 50 and 100; 200 and 300 are added to show the trend (all are valid because $k < \min(1400, |V|)$). Runtimes are wall-clock seconds on this machine: fit = SVD of the document matrix (for TF-IDF: preprocessing + building the matrix, which LSA also needs before its SVD), query = transforming/folding the 225 queries, cosine scoring and sorting all 1,400 documents. Times are medians of 3 runs.

Discussion — effect of the number of dimensions.

k explained variance P@5 MAP nDCG@10 vs. TF-IDF
20 18.7 % 0.170 0.207 0.234 much worse: 20 topics are too coarse for 225 specific technical queries
50 31.2 % 0.228 0.269 0.307 worse on every metric (−8 % MAP, −12 % nDCG@10)
100 43.9 % 0.266 0.302 0.353 about equal (MAP +3.6 %, nDCG@10 +1.0 %, P@5 −3 %)
200 59.8 % 0.286 0.319 0.382 best: P@5 +4.3 %, MAP +9.4 %, nDCG@10 +9.2 %
300 70.4 % 0.281 0.313 0.371 still better, but falling back toward TF-IDF
  • Retrieval quality first rises with k and then falls slightly. Small k merges too many concepts (the qid 136 effect). As k approaches the rank of the matrix, LSA becomes TF-IDF again and loses its smoothing benefit. For this small, technical collection the best value is around k ≈ 200. The k = 50 suggested in the lab handout is too aggressive here.
  • Explained variance is low: 50 components keep only 31 % of the variance, because a short-abstract TF-IDF matrix is very sparse and high-rank. Explained variance alone is therefore a poor guide for choosing k, and it should be tuned on retrieval metrics.
  • The randomized SVD is stable: over 5 seeds the k = 50 metrics vary by at most ±0.003.
  • Runtime (table above). The SVD (indexing) cost grows roughly linearly with k, from about 0.1 s at k = 20 to over 1 s at k = 300, on top of building the TF-IDF matrix. Query time (folding in, scoring and sorting 225 queries) stays at a few tens of milliseconds for every configuration. At this scale it is dominated by sorting, so it hardly changes with k. On a large collection the dense k-dimensional document vectors would be much smaller than the sparse vocabulary-sized vectors, but they could no longer be searched with an inverted index.

Part 4 — Word embeddings with Word2Vec¶

Training corpus. The same 1,400 documents (title + abstract), split into sentences at full stops, lower-cased, tokenised with the same tokenizer and stop-word list as Part 1. Stemming is not applied here so that nearest neighbours are readable words (e.g. aerodynamic rather than the stem aerodynam).

Configurations (identical except the architecture):

parameter value
vector_size 100
window 5
min_count 5 (words seen fewer than 5 times get unreliable vectors on a corpus this small)
negative sampling 10 (no hierarchical softmax)
sample (down-sampling) 1e-3
epochs 30 (the corpus is small, ~130k tokens, so many passes are needed)
sg 0 = CBOW, 1 = Skip-gram

workers=1, a fixed seed and a deterministic hash function make the runs reproducible.

In [19]:
def sentences_of(text):
    for s in re.split(r"\s\.\s|\s\.$|\.\s", text.lower()):
        toks = tokenize(s)
        if len(toks) >= 2:
            yield toks

sentences = [s for t in docs_df["text"] for s in sentences_of(t)]
n_tok = sum(len(s) for s in sentences)
print(f"sentences: {len(sentences):,}   tokens: {n_tok:,}   distinct words: {len(set(w for s in sentences for w in s)):,}")
print("example:", sentences[0])

def stable_hash(s):
    return zlib.crc32(s.encode("utf-8"))

W2V_PARAMS = dict(vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=5, negative=10, hs=0, sample=1e-3,
                  epochs=30, workers=1, seed=SEED, hashfxn=stable_hash)
models, train_times = {}, {}
for name, sg in [("CBOW", 0), ("Skip-gram", 1)]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    models[name] = Word2Vec(sentences=sentences, sg=sg, **W2V_PARAMS)
    train_times[name] = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"{name:9s}: vocabulary {len(models[name].wv):,} words, training time {train_times[name]:.1f} s")
w2v_vocab = models["CBOW"].wv.index_to_key
RESULTS["w2v"] = {"sentences": len(sentences), "tokens": n_tok, "vocab": len(w2v_vocab),
                  "train_time_s": train_times}

CBOW vs Skip-gram.

  • Neighbour type. CBOW (which predicts a word from the average of its context) returns words that can replace the target in a sentence: supersonic → transonic, subsonic; buckling → deformations, wrinkling, buckle; aerofoil → airfoil, wings, delta. Skip-gram (which predicts each context word from the target) returns more topical associates, including rarer, specific words: heat → transfer, shield, refractory, transpiration (the heat-shield topic); buckling → rings, unstiffened, stiffened, postbuckling; shock → wave, attenuation, incident.
  • Agreement. Only about 21 % of the top-10 neighbours are shared on average (Jaccard 0.207 over the 1,000 most frequent words), so the two architectures learn noticeably different spaces from the same 130k tokens.
  • Separation. Both give clearly higher cosine to the hand-picked related pairs than to random pairs. CBOW has the larger gap (0.405 vs 0.294). Skip-gram gives even random pairs a fairly high cosine (0.20), so its similarity values must be read relative to that baseline.
  • Cost. Skip-gram makes one prediction per (word, context word) pair instead of one per window, so it trained about 3× slower than CBOW (see the training times in the table, one thread).

4.2 Comparison with count-based word similarity¶

Two count-based term representations are built on the same unstemmed tokens and vocabulary as Word2Vec:

  • TF-IDF (document-level) — each word is a column of the document–term TF-IDF matrix; two words are similar when they occur in the same documents (first-order co-occurrence / word overlap).
  • PPMI co-occurrence (window-level) — word × context counts within a ±5 word window inside sentences, re-weighted by positive pointwise mutual information; each word is a row, compared with cosine.
In [22]:
w_index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(w2v_vocab)}
V = len(w2v_vocab)

# (a) TF-IDF term vectors: columns of a doc x word TF-IDF matrix over the unstemmed vocabulary
tfidf_words = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer=lambda t: [w for w in tokenize(t) if w in w_index])
Xw = tfidf_words.fit_transform(docs_df["text"])
term_vecs_tfidf = Xw.T.tocsr()
tfidf_w_index = tfidf_words.vocabulary_

# (b) PPMI over a +-5 word window
rows_, cols_ = [], []
for s in sentences:
    ids = [w_index[w] for w in s if w in w_index]
    for i, wi in enumerate(ids):
        for j in range(max(0, i - 5), min(len(ids), i + 6)):
            if j != i:
                rows_.append(wi); cols_.append(ids[j])
C = sp.coo_matrix((np.ones(len(rows_)), (rows_, cols_)), shape=(V, V)).tocsr()
total = C.sum()
row_sum = np.asarray(C.sum(1)).ravel(); col_sum = np.asarray(C.sum(0)).ravel()
Cc = C.tocoo()
pmi = np.log((Cc.data * total) / (row_sum[Cc.row] * col_sum[Cc.col]))
keep = pmi > 0
PPMI = sp.csr_matrix((pmi[keep], (Cc.row[keep], Cc.col[keep])), shape=(V, V))
print(f"TF-IDF word matrix: {Xw.shape};  co-occurrence matrix: {C.shape}, PPMI non-zeros: {PPMI.nnz:,}")

# Document frequency and number of documents in which two words co-occur (word overlap)
doc_sets = [set(tokenize(t)) for t in docs_df["text"]]
def df_both(a, b):
    return sum(1 for s in doc_sets if a in s and b in s)

def count_neighbours(mat, idx, inv, w, n=5):
    v = mat[idx[w]]
    sims = cosine_similarity(v, mat).ravel()
    sims[idx[w]] = -1
    top = np.argsort(-sims)[:n]
    return [(inv[i], float(sims[i])) for i in top]

inv_tfidf = {i: w for w, i in tfidf_w_index.items()}
inv_w = dict(enumerate(w2v_vocab))
rows = []
for t in TERMS:
    rows.append({"term": t,
                 "TF-IDF (same documents)": nn_str(count_neighbours(term_vecs_tfidf, tfidf_w_index, inv_tfidf, t)),
                 "PPMI (window co-occurrence)": nn_str(count_neighbours(PPMI, w_index, inv_w, t)),
                 "Skip-gram": nn_str(models["Skip-gram"].wv.most_similar(t, topn=5))})
count_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("term")
count_table.to_csv(OUT / "tables" / "count_vs_w2v_neighbours.csv")
display(count_table)
RESULTS["count_neighbours"] = count_table.reset_index().to_dict("records")

def cos_tfidf(a, b):
    return float(cosine_similarity(term_vecs_tfidf[tfidf_w_index[a]], term_vecs_tfidf[tfidf_w_index[b]])[0, 0])
def cos_ppmi(a, b):
    return float(cosine_similarity(PPMI[w_index[a]], PPMI[w_index[b]])[0, 0])
lsa_term_vecs = lsa_runs[100]["svd"].components_.T * lsa_runs[100]["svd"].singular_values_
def cos_lsa(a, b):
    ia, ib = tfidf.vocabulary_[stem(a)], tfidf.vocabulary_[stem(b)]
    return float(cosine_similarity(lsa_term_vecs[[ia]], lsa_term_vecs[[ib]])[0, 0])

Count-based vs embedding similarity.

  • TF-IDF (document-level) neighbours are words that appear in the same abstracts. These are topical associates such as supersonic → flow, speeds, mach, theory, pressure, and the score is high only when the two words actually co-occur in documents (heat–transfer 0.83, shock–wave 0.54).
  • PPMI (window-level) neighbours are already closer to Word2Vec (supersonic → subsonic, wing → wings, tail, chord, flaps), because they also use local context instead of whole documents.
  • The rank correlation table supports this. Word2Vec similarities correlate more with window PPMI (ρ ≈ 0.52–0.54) than with document TF-IDF (ρ ≈ 0.37–0.40). This is consistent with the known result that skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorises a (shifted) PMI word–context matrix.
  • The pair table shows the main difference. Words that substitute for each other but seldom appear in the same abstract get almost zero TF-IDF similarity: aerofoil–airfoil 0.013, wing–aerofoil 0.035, supersonic–hypersonic 0.086. CBOW gives them 0.46–0.49. Pairs that co-occur constantly (shock–wave, temperature–heat) score well under every method. LSA term vectors (k = 100) behave like smoothed TF-IDF: they help when the documents themselves overlap (viscous–inviscid 0.27 → 0.56, shock–wave 0.54 → 0.72) but not for the spelling variants. Stemming, on the other hand, trivially merges plate/plates (cos 1.0).

4.3 A relationship that embeddings capture but word overlap misses¶

Search systematically for such cases: among the Skip-gram top-10 neighbours of frequent words, find pairs with high embedding similarity but that rarely or never appear in the same document (so their document-level TF-IDF similarity is low).

Example — "aerofoil" vs "airfoil". The Cranfield abstracts use both the British spelling aerofoil (18 documents) and the American spelling airfoil (53 documents) for the same object. Only one document contains both, so any method based on word overlap treats them as unrelated:

  • exact matching / TF-IDF: the stems differ (aerofoil ≠ airfoil), so a query that says airfoil gets no credit from a document that says aerofoil. The document-level TF-IDF cosine of the two words is 0.013;
  • LSA (k = 100): −0.03. The two spellings occur in disjoint sets of documents, so the document-level SVD does not connect them either.

CBOW puts airfoil as the nearest neighbour of aerofoil (rank 1 of 2,696 words, cosine 0.49). Word2Vec never needs the two words to occur together. It only needs them to occur in similar contexts, and both appear next to theory, pressure, lift, distribution, section, mach, velocity, transonic, flow (the shared-context list above). Because CBOW is trained to predict a word from its context, two words that fill the same slot get similar vectors. This is a second-order (distributional) relation, which first-order word overlap cannot see. The same effect gives pairs such as diameter–width and integration–solving (0 shared documents, Skip-gram cosine ≈ 0.55) in the systematic search above.

In retrieval this matters for queries 42 and 43 ("transonic flow around an airfoil"): relevant doc 468 only says aerofoil. TF-IDF still finds it (ranks 6 and 12), but only through the other shared words (transonic, flow), not through the key term. Expanding the query with Word2Vec neighbours would close that gap.

Skip-gram ranks airfoil only 450th for aerofoil. With just 35 occurrences of aerofoil, Skip-gram fits the word's specific co-occurring terms (split, discs, inverted) instead of its general slot. On a corpus this small, CBOW's context averaging gives the more robust substitute relation.

Note: Word2Vec vectors are static, one vector per word type learnt from its contexts. Fully contextual models such as BERT would also tell apart different senses of the same word in different sentences.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
groups = {"flow regime": ["supersonic", "hypersonic", "subsonic", "transonic", "incompressible"],
          "boundary layer": ["laminar", "turbulent", "transition", "separation", "skin"],
          "structures": ["buckling", "shells", "plates", "stresses", "elastic"],
          "lifting surfaces": ["wing", "aerofoil", "airfoil", "delta", "swept"],
          "heat transfer": ["heat", "temperature", "conduction", "transfer", "radiation"]}
words = [w for g in groups.values() for w in g if w in models["Skip-gram"].wv]
P = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=SEED).fit_transform(models["Skip-gram"].wv[words])
colors = dict(zip(groups, ["#2a6fb0", "#c0504d", "#4f9a4f", "#8064a2", "#d08a1e"]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.2))
for g, ws in groups.items():
    idx = [words.index(w) for w in ws if w in words]
    ax.scatter(P[idx, 0], P[idx, 1], color=colors[g], label=g, s=30)
    for i in idx:
        ax.annotate(words[i], P[i], fontsize=8, xytext=(3, 3), textcoords="offset points")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_title("Skip-gram embeddings (PCA projection)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(OUT / "figures" / "skipgram_pca.png", dpi=150); plt.close()
display(Image(str(OUT / "figures" / "skipgram_pca.png")))

Conclusions¶

  1. TF-IDF baseline: 1,400 documents, 225 queries (222 with relevant documents), a 4,170-stem vocabulary and a 1400 × 4170 matrix that is 98.7 % sparse. It reaches P@5 0.274, MAP 0.291, nDCG@10 0.350.
  2. LSA (k = 50): keeps 31 % of the variance and places documents (1400 × 50) and queries (225 × 50) in a dense latent space. It is worse than TF-IDF on this collection (MAP 0.269, nDCG@10 0.307). It helps queries whose relevant documents use different vocabulary (qid 184: nDCG@10 0 → 0.70), and it hurts precise queries where a rare term picks out the relevant paper within a cluster of similar ones (qid 136: AP 1.0 → 0.13).
  3. Dimensionality: quality peaks at k ≈ 200 (P@5 0.286, MAP 0.319, nDCG@10 0.382, about +9 % MAP/nDCG over TF-IDF). k = 100 ties with the baseline, and k = 20 and 50 are too coarse. Indexing cost grows with k, while query cost stays well under 1 ms per query.
  4. Word2Vec: CBOW gives substitutable neighbours (supersonic → transonic, subsonic), and Skip-gram gives topical associates (heat → transfer, shield, refractory). Both agree more with window-based PPMI than with document-level TF-IDF. Embeddings capture relations that word overlap misses, such as the spelling variants aerofoil/airfoil (TF-IDF cosine 0.01, CBOW nearest neighbour).
